title: String Operations
overview: Text is everywhere in programming — user names, emails, messages, file paths. Python treats strings as first-class citizens with a rich set of built-in tools. In this lecture, you'll master string manipulation and formatting.

blocks.content: A **string** is a sequence of characters. Think of it as a chain of beads — each character is one bead, positioned at a specific index.
Since strings are sequences, everything you learned about list indexing and slicing applies here too.

blocks.title: Try It — String Indexing and Slicing
blocks.code:
name = "Lakshanya"

print(name[0])      # First character: L
print(name[-1])     # Last character: a
print(name[0:4])    # First 4: Laks
print(name[4:])     # From index 4 onwards
print(len(name))    # Length: 9

blocks.content: Strings in Python are **immutable** — you cannot change individual characters. But you can build new strings.

**Common string operations:**

`+` Concatenation · `*` Repetition · `in` Membership check

blocks.title: Try It — String Operations
blocks.code:
first = "Python"
second = " 2.0"

# Concatenation
full = first + second
print(full)

# Repetition
print("-" * 20)

# Membership
print("Py" in first)   # True
print("Java" in first) # False

analogy.title: Beaded Necklace
analogy.description: A string of beads — each bead is a character at a position. You can view any bead by its position (index), pull out a section of beads (slice), or check if a particular bead is in the necklace (in). You can't replace a single bead, but you can create a new necklace.
bullets: Each bead has a fixed position — bead 0, bead 1, bead 2...
You can access any single bead by counting to its position.
The necklace is fixed in order — you can't rearrange the beads.
analogy.highlightCard: A string is a sequence of characters — each one has an index, just like beads.

visualization.title: String as Indexed Sequence
bullets: name[0] gives the first character, name[-1] gives the last.
name[1:4] slices characters at positions 1, 2, and 3.
len(name) counts the total number of characters in the string.
visualization.highlightCard: Strings are sequences — index and slice them exactly like lists.

code.output: P y t h o n
highlights: name[0] returns 'R' — the character at position 0.
name[0:3] returns 'Roh' — characters at index 0, 1, and 2.
Strings are immutable — you can read characters but cannot change them.
code.highlightCard: String indexing and slicing give you precise control over any text value.

reflection.question: What does 'abc' * 3 produce?
reflection.answer: 'abcabcabc' — the * operator repeats the string that many times.

blocks.stage1Transition: Python strings are indexed exactly like lists. Let's explore string indexing and slicing.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how string indexing and slicing work in Python.
blocks.takeaway: A necklace is a perfect string — ordered beads with fixed positions. Python strings work identically: each character has an index, you can access or slice any portion.

blocks.title: Name Formatter
blocks.instructions: Ask for a first name and last name. Create a formatted name card that prints: LASTNAME, Firstname (uppercase last name, title case first name). Also print the total character count of the full name (without the comma and space).
blocks.starterCode:
first = input("First name: ")
last = input("Last name: ")

# Format and print
print(last.upper() + ", " + first.title())
print("Character count:", len(first) + len(last))
blocks.solution:
first = input("First name: ")
last = input("Last name: ")

print(last.upper() + ", " + first.title())
print("Character count:", len(first) + len(last))
blocks.hint: Use .upper() and .title() methods directly on the strings.
blocks.expectedOutput:
First name: Last name: KRISHNAN, Lakshanya
Character count: 18

blocks.content: Python strings come loaded with methods — built-in operations you can call directly on any string.

blocks.title: Try It — Case and Search Methods
blocks.code:
text = "  Hello, Python World!  "

# Case methods
print(text.lower())
print(text.upper())
print(text.title())

# Stripping whitespace
print(text.strip())    # Both ends
print(text.lstrip())   # Left only
print(text.rstrip())   # Right only
blocks.expectedOutput:
hello, python world!  
  HELLO, PYTHON WORLD!  
  Hello, Python World!  
Hello, Python World!
Hello, Python World!  
  Hello, Python World!

blocks.title: Try It — Find, Replace, Split, Join
blocks.code:
sentence = "Python is fun and Python is powerful"

# Find
print(sentence.find("Python"))    # First occurrence index
print(sentence.count("Python"))   # Count occurrences

# Replace
print(sentence.replace("Python", "Coding"))

# Split into list
words = sentence.split(" ")
print(words[:4])

# Join list back into string
print("-".join(["a", "b", "c"]))
blocks.expectedOutput:
0
2
Coding is fun and Coding is powerful
['Python', 'is', 'fun', 'and']
a-b-c

analogy.title: Word Processor
analogy.description: Think of string methods as the tools in a word processor: Format > Uppercase is .upper(), Find & Replace is .replace(), autocorrect removes whitespace like .strip(). You're editing text with purpose-built tools.
bullets: Make all text UPPERCASE for a heading, lowercase for body text.
Find and replace a word across the entire document instantly.
Count the total characters, split text into paragraphs, or strip extra spaces.
analogy.highlightCard: String methods are built-in tools for transforming and analyzing text.

visualization.title: String Methods by Purpose
bullets: upper() and lower() convert case — useful for comparisons and display.
strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace from user input.
replace('old', 'new') substitutes text throughout the string.
visualization.highlightCard: upper, lower, strip, replace, split — five string methods every Python developer uses daily.

highlights: name.upper() returns a new ALL-CAPS string — the original is unchanged.
sentence.replace('hello', 'hi') returns a new string with replacements.
sentence.split(' ') splits the string into a list of words at each space.
code.highlightCard: String methods return new strings — they never modify the original.

reflection.question: What does .split() return?
reflection.answer: A list of substrings. By default it splits on whitespace. You can specify a delimiter: 'a,b,c'.split(',') returns ['a', 'b', 'c'].

blocks.stage1Transition: Python has powerful built-in string methods. Let's explore the most essential ones.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how the most important string methods work in Python.
blocks.takeaway: A word processor shows every string method in action — uppercase headings (upper), find-replace (replace), word count (split + len). Python has all of these built in and ready to use.

blocks.title: Email Cleaner
blocks.instructions: Users sometimes submit emails with extra spaces and wrong capitalisation. Clean this email: '   USER.NAME@EXAMPLE.COM   '. Strip whitespace and convert to lowercase. Then check if it ends with '@example.com' and print True/False.
blocks.starterCode:
raw_email = "   USER.NAME@EXAMPLE.COM   "

# Clean the email
clean =

print("Valid domain:", clean.endswith("@example.com"))

blocks.content: You've already seen f-strings. But Python has more formatting options, and f-strings can do much more than basic variable insertion.

blocks.title: Try It — Advanced f-strings
blocks.code:
name = "Priya"
marks = 87.5678

# Basic
print(f"Student: {name}")

# Decimal precision: .2f = 2 decimal places
print(f"Average: {marks:.2f}")

# Width and alignment
print(f"{name:<15} {marks:>8.2f}")  # Left, Right align
print(f"{'---':-^20}")              # Center with fill char

blocks.title: Try It — Building a Formatted Table
blocks.code:
students = [("Arjun", 92), ("Priya", 87), ("Ravi", 78)]

print(f"{'Name':<12} {'Marks':>6}")
print("-" * 20)
for name, mark in students:
    print(f"{name:<12} {mark:>6}")

analogy.title: Restaurant Menu Layout
analogy.description: A menu aligns dish names on the left and prices on the right. f-strings with alignment formatting do exactly this — control where text appears so your output looks professional and readable.
bullets: The menu formats dish names in consistent columns and aligns prices on the right.
Each dish is described in a standard width to keep the layout clean.
Consistent formatting makes the menu look professional and easy to read.
analogy.highlightCard: f-string format codes control alignment, width, and decimal places precisely.

visualization.title: f-string Format Codes
bullets: {name:<15} left-aligns text in a field of 15 characters.
{price:.2f} displays a float with exactly 2 decimal places.
{:>10} right-aligns text — useful for columns of numbers.
visualization.highlightCard: f"{name:<15} {price:.2f}" — perfect for formatted tables, reports, and menus.

highlights: :<15 pads the string to 15 characters and left-aligns it.
:.2f rounds the float to exactly 2 decimal places.
Combining both in one f-string creates a perfectly aligned table row.
code.highlightCard: f-string format codes turn raw data into beautiful, professional-looking output.

reflection.question: What does {value:.2f} do in an f-string?
reflection.answer: Formats the number as a float with exactly 2 decimal places, rounding if necessary.

blocks.stage1Transition: Python's f-string format codes let you control how values are displayed. Let's see them.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how f-string format codes produce clean output in Python.
blocks.takeaway: A restaurant menu is perfectly formatted — consistent spacing, aligned prices, clean columns. Python f-string format codes give you the same control over every output your program produces.

blocks.title: Formatted Invoice
blocks.instructions:
Create a formatted invoice with a header and two items. Use f-strings with alignment so that item names are left-aligned in 20 chars and prices are right-aligned in 8 chars.

Item: 'Python Textbook' — price: 450.5
Item: 'USB Hub' — price: 799.99
Print total at the bottom.
blocks.starterCode:
items = [("Python Textbook", 450.5), ("USB Hub", 799.99)]

print(f"{'Item':<20} {'Price':>8}")
print("-" * 30)

total = 0
for name, price in items:
    print(f"{name:<20} {price:>8.2f}")
    total += price

print("-" * 30)
print(f"{'Total':<20} {total:>8.2f}")
blocks.solution:
items = [("Python Textbook", 450.5), ("USB Hub", 799.99)]

print(f"{'Item':<20} {'Price':>8}")
print("-" * 30)

for name, price in items:
    print(f"{name:<20} {price:>8.2f}")

print(f"{'Total':<20} {total:>8.2f}")
blocks.hint: Use :<20 for left-align name, :>8.2f for right-align price with 2 decimals.

keyTakeaways.text: Strings are indexed sequences — use [i] for characters, [i:j] for slices.
Strings are immutable — you can't change them in place, but you can create new ones.
Case methods: .upper(), .lower(), .title() — return a new string.
.strip() removes leading/trailing whitespace — essential for cleaning user input.
.split() converts a string into a list. .join() converts a list back into a string.
f-string format codes: :.2f for decimals, :<n left-align, :>n right-align.

whatYouLearned: How to index and slice strings
Essential string methods: upper, lower, strip, find, replace, split, join
How to use advanced f-string formatting for aligned, decimal-controlled output

quiz.question: What does 'Hello World'.split() return?
quiz.explanation: .split() without arguments splits on whitespace and returns a list. 'Hello World' has one space, producing two elements: ['Hello', 'World'].

quiz.question: What does '  hello  '.strip() return?
quiz.explanation: .strip() removes leading AND trailing whitespace from both ends of the string, returning the clean inner text.

quiz.question: What will f'{3.14159:.2f}' produce?
quiz.explanation: :.2f formats the number as a float with exactly 2 decimal places. 3.14159 rounded to 2 decimals is 3.14.

quiz.question: How do you join a list ['a', 'b', 'c'] into the string 'a-b-c'?
quiz.explanation: .join() is called on the separator string and takes the iterable as an argument. The separator is placed between each item.

quiz.question: Are strings mutable in Python?
options: Yes, you can change individual characters
No, but you can create new strings from old ones
Only if they're longer than 10 characters
quiz.answer: No, but you can create new strings from old ones
quiz.explanation: Strings in Python are immutable. You can't do name[0] = 'J'. But methods like .replace() and .upper() return NEW strings — the original is unchanged.

problems.title: Palindrome Checker
problems.description:
Write a function is_palindrome(text) that returns True if the text reads the same forwards and backwards (ignoring spaces and case).

Test:
is_palindrome('racecar') → True
is_palindrome('hello') → False
is_palindrome('A man a plan a canal Panama') → True
problems.starterCode:
def is_palindrome(text):
    # Clean: lowercase and remove spaces
    clean = text.lower().replace(" ", "")
    # Check if it reads the same backwards
    return clean == clean[::-1]

print(is_palindrome("racecar"))
print(is_palindrome("hello"))
print(is_palindrome("A man a plan a canal Panama"))
problems.solution:
def is_palindrome(text):
    clean = text.lower().replace(" ", "")
    return clean == clean[::-1]

print(is_palindrome("racecar"))
print(is_palindrome("hello"))
print(is_palindrome("A man a plan a canal Panama"))

problems.title: String Statistics
problems.description:
Given a sentence, print:
1. Number of words
2. Number of unique words
3. Longest word
4. Most common starting letter

Sentence: 'the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog the'
problems.starterCode:
sentence = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog the"
words = sentence.split()

# 1. Word count
print(f"Words: {len(words)}")

# 2. Unique words
print(f"Unique: {len(set(words))}")

# 3. Longest word
print(f"Longest: {max(words, key=len)}")

# 4. Most common starting letter
letters = [w[0] for w in words]
print(f"Most common start: {max(set(letters), key=letters.count)}")
problems.solution:
sentence = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog the"
words = sentence.split()

print(f"Words: {len(words)}")
print(f"Unique: {len(set(words))}")
print(f"Longest: {max(words, key=len)}")

letters = [w[0] for w in words]
print(f"Most common start: {max(set(letters), key=letters.count)}")
